meta.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?
meta.subtitle: Assessment of the Parcelbird Now proposal and recommendation to the board · Board meeting, January 2027
meta.purpose: Decide whether to launch Parcelbird Now in 2027
meta.confidentiality: Prepared from the board briefing pack only (synthetic benchmark data); no external research

Choices made without the user (unavailable)
inputs.content: Mode: compile, restructure (given). Audience: board deciding approve/decline. Theme: navy (recommended default). Analysis thresholds kept as stated and flagged.

storyline.governing_thought: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash

exec_summary.text: The market is growing fast, but no operator makes money in it

sub_points.text: Sales grew 42% a year in 2022–25, yet both incumbents lose money on every order

exec_summary.text: A Parcelbird store would lose money on every order, and customers don't stay long enough to repay their acquisition cost

sub_points.text: A store loses $6.17 per order at the median; only the founders' plan, beyond any site observed, makes money
Our pop-up lost $12.57 per order, and only 22% of its customers still ordered in month 3

exec_summary.text: Even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the investors' cash constraints

sub_points.text: It needs $9.5M against $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; with core burn, cash runs out in month 13

exec_summary.text: The software business is a better use of the same cash

sub_points.text: It breaks even in about month 26 at today's 60% growth and month 36 at 40%
It keeps 12 months of runway as long as ARR grows 34% a year or more

exec_summary.text: Decline the launch, back software-first in phased steps, and set triggers for any return to quick commerce

sub_points.text: The launch case meets none of its six conditions; a 90-day checkpoint gates the second tranche of hires

next_steps.action: Record the decision to decline the 2027 launch and close the pop-up; keep its data and cohort learning
Release the first tranche of software hires against signed late-stage contracts (9 grocers, $0.86M ARR)
Stand up the quarterly re-entry trigger dashboard and monthly runway report against the 12-month rule
Test a store-based fast-delivery offer with late-stage pipeline accounts
90-day checkpoint: ARR growth against the 34% minimum; hold the second tranche if below

units.text: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash
US quick-commerce GMV grew 42% a year, 2022–25 ($1.8B to $5.1B)
Both incumbents lose money on every order: EBITDA margins −26% and −46%, contribution −$1.90 and −$3.40
QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities (36%) in 2025; Zipcart positive only in its densest city after a fee rise
'Nobody owns the Midwest' may mean nobody has made it pay; growth does not justify entry on its own
Median store loses $6.17 per order, $2.67 before site cost, so more volume cannot fix it
Riders $7.40 per order, 81% of goods margin; two of three cities considering minimum pay
Only the founders' plan (+$2.02) makes money; best observed on every driver loses $1.76; pop-up −$12.57
No site achieved the best-observed case: best AOV and best density come from different sites
Nine stores: −$18.2M a year at the median, −$8.1M best observed, +$11.9M on the plan
Break-even AOV: $63 median store, $50 best observed, against $34 and $42
Plan beats the best site ever observed on all four drivers (+7%, −4 pp, +17%, +29%)
Scale check: plan sales of $266M a year exceed QuickBasket's $210M and are about 5% of the US market
If AOV or rider productivity only reaches the median, the plan loses money; density or promotions alone leave about $0.2–0.3
The pop-up was below the median on every driver; no evidence of a capability edge
Fair caveat: six weeks on a temporary site; orders grew 18% a week (about 179 to 408 a day), bought with 12% promotions and $38 CAC
Ramp-up alone does not close the gap
44% stated weekly intent against 22% still ordering in month 3 at 3.1 orders a month (0.68 per acquired customer)
$38 CAC is never repaid at median or pop-up economics; best observed 77 orders / 113 months; plan 10 orders / 15 months
Buying growth with promotions and paid social does not create value at these economics
Zipcart's profitable city needed a $3.99 fee, 1% promotions and lost 14% of volume; the same moves leave our median store at −$1.05
With Zipcart's moves a median store earns +$3.02 before site cost and needs about 1,042 orders a day: 16% above median, 3.7 times the pop-up
The launch needs $9.5M; only $7.2M can be spent above the 12-month runway floor ($2.3M short)
With core burn added, runway falls below 12 months in month 5 and cash runs out in month 13
Even if the $9.5M covered all spending, $2.5M is left at month 18: about 6 months of runway against 12
At benchmark economics 9 stores lose about $18M a year ($1.5M a month); a new round is 'unlikely'
The runway floor rises once stores operate, so the $7.2M headroom is a ceiling
Of three options (launch, pilot store, software-first), only software-first meets both investor constraints and keeps a foothold in fast delivery
Pilot store: $0.6M capex plus about $2.0M a year of losses, breaches the runway rule in month 10, little new learning
Cash: A runs out in month 13 (low −$2.5M); B drifts to $0.2M; C bottoms at $5.4M and never breaches the runway rule
Cash model assumptions: opex flat apart from hires; A's spend phasing; B at median economics; runway = cash ÷ recurring burn
Software-first by growth: break-even month 26/36/41, low $5.4M/$2.7M/$1.2M, min runway 24/18/12 months at 60/40/34%; 25% runs out
Software-first holds only while ARR grows at least 34% a year
Break-even ARR = $8.9M ÷ 0.81 = $11.0M, against $4.1M today
Pipeline: 9 late-stage grocers worth $0.86M of ARR, all 37 worth $3.55M; the hires pay for themselves with 10 contracts (28%)
34% growth means about 15 net new contracts in year 1 (26 at 60%); costs flat apart from hires; no churn or win rates, so phase hires
The founders' hypothesis fails all six conditions it needs; it is reversed
The recommendation survives the main uncertainties: most make a launch worse; main risk to C is growth below 34%, managed by phased hires

Four re-entry triggers: site-level profit two quarters; drivers together (AOV ≥ $42, ≥ 3.0 orders/rider-hour, ≥ 1,050 orders a day, or fee losing ≤ 15% volume); payback within 12 months; ring-fenced funding
Four decisions: decline launch and pop-up extension; approve $0.8M of hires in two tranches; build store-based fast-delivery offer; adopt triggers and runway reporting (owners and dates)
90-day checkpoint (April 2027); hold the second tranche of hires if growth tracks below 34%
Judgement calls where the pack is ambiguous; none changes the answer
